ta-l1d6q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 6–7, where Lombard turns from the supposit and terminus of generation to its principle. Distinction 6 asks whether the principle is necessity, will, or nature; Distinction 7 asks whether the power of begetting is common to Father and Son. Thomas maps Lombard's answer ('neither by will nor by necessity'), his response to an objection, his interpretation of it, and his rejection of Eunomius's 'laughable dialectic', which would make the divine nature mutable, together with the sharp reply to a cunning heretic. Three articles are announced: whether the Father begot the Son by necessity, by will, or by nature.
claims: Lombard denies that the Father begot the Son either by will or by necessity, against Eunomius.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e131.summary: First argument that the Father begot by necessity. Necessary and possible divide being, so if the Father did not beget by necessity he begot contingently or possibly, which is impossible.
claims: Being is divided into necessary and possible.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e134.summary: Second argument. Everything eternal is necessary, and the Son's generation is eternal.
claims: Whatever is eternal is necessary.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e137.summary: Third argument. As God is good per se, he is necessary being per se, since whatever is by participation reduces to what is per se. In what is good per se there is only good, so in what is necessary per se there is only the necessary, and generation in God is necessary.
claims: In the per se necessary there is nothing but the necessary.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e141.summary: Contrary argument. All necessity comes from something compelling, inwardly or outwardly, and nothing can be stronger than God.
claims: Necessity arises from something compelling, and nothing is stronger than God.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e144.summary: Second contrary argument. Augustine divides necessity into coercion and prohibition, and neither befits God.
claims: Necessity is either coercion or prohibition.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e147.summary: Thomas's determination, after the Philosopher's senses of 'necessary'. Some necessity is conditional: from the agent, by violence (one forced to run must run only on condition of the force), or from the end, as what is required for the end, either for being (food) or for well-being (a ship for crossing the sea). Absolute necessity is what is necessary by what is in its essence, whether the essence itself (in simple things) or a principle of it, matter (humans must die) or form (humans are rational). Absolute necessity is either received from another, as in all caused things, or uncaused and the cause of necessity in all else, as in God. Divine generation has no conditional necessity, from agent or end, since God is first principle and last end. It is necessary with the absolute necessity of the first cause.
claims: Necessity is conditional (from the agent by violence, or from the end) or absolute (from what is in a thing's essence).
Absolute necessity is either received from another or uncaused, as in God.
Divine generation is necessary with the absolute, uncaused necessity of the first cause, not by coercion or for an end.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e150.summary: Answers both sides. The first arguments concern absolute necessity, which holds. The contrary ones concern the necessity of coercion, which conflicts with absolute necessity. The heretic was arguing from coercion, and that is what Lombard's text denies.
claims: Lombard denies coercive necessity of the generation, not absolute necessity.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e162.summary: First argument that the Father begot by will. Every good is willed by God as every truth is known, and the Son's generation is the best of goods.
claims: Every good is willed by God.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e165.summary: Second argument. In human generation the principle inclining to generate is the will, and human generation is derived from the divine, so divine generation is by will too.
claims: Human generation proceeds from will and derives from divine generation.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e168.summary: Third argument from Origen, who says the Father, bringing forth the offspring of his will, became Father of the Word. The offspring of will is born by the will of the begetter.
claims: Origen calls the Word the offspring of the Father's will.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e175.summary: Contrary argument. In human affairs will is the principle of producing artifacts, but the Son is produced not as an artifact but as the art itself, whereas creatures are produced as artifacts. So the Father produced creatures by will but did not beget the Son by will.
claims: Will produces artifacts; the Son proceeds as art, creatures as artifacts.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e178.summary: Second contrary argument from Hilary: anathema to anyone who says the Son was made by the will of God like a made thing.
claims: Hilary condemns saying the Son was made by God's will.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e184.summary: Thomas's determination. Will relates to something either as power to object or as principle. As to object, whatever God wills can be said to be by his will: the Father is God by his will, since he wills to be God, and in this sense he begot the Son by will. As principle, there are two cases. The will may be the formal ground of the principiating, as it is for the procession of the Spirit, who proceeds as love, the love by which the will produces all creatures; in the same way the intellect relates to the generation of the Son, who proceeds as Word and art. Or the thing produced may proceed from the will according to the will's condition, which is freedom, so its products are only things that can be or not be. In this sense the divine will relates to creation, not to the Son's generation. Hence a threefold distinction. Supervening will, newly added to the work, is not in God at all. Concomitant will, relating only to the object, is in God with respect to the Son's generation. Antecedent will, relating principle to product, concerns creatures.
claims: The Father begot the Son by will only in the sense of concomitant will, the will as relating to its object.
The will is the principle of the Spirit's procession as love and of creation as free production; the intellect is the principle of the Son's generation as Word.
Supervening will is not in God; concomitant will concerns the generation; antecedent will concerns creatures.
concepts: procession as love and as word

ta-l1d6q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the first argument. It proceeds only from the relation of will to its object.
claims: God wills the generation only as object, not as its principle.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the second argument. Human generation is not eternal and can have an antecedent will, which divine generation cannot.
claims: Antecedent will presupposes non-eternal production.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e193.summary: Reply to the third argument. By 'offspring of will' Origen means that in which the Father's good pleasure rests, the Son ('This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased', Matt. 3:17). The contrary arguments concern antecedent will, the relation of principle to product.
claims: The Son is the 'offspring of will' as the one in whom the Father's good pleasure rests.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e208.summary: First argument that the Father did not beget by nature. Hilary says the Father did not beget the Son led by natural necessity.
claims: Hilary denies natural necessity in the generation.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e214.summary: Second argument. In God will and nature are the same, and the Father did not beget by will, so not by nature either.
claims: Will and nature are identical in God.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e217.summary: Third argument. The philosophers could reach knowledge of the divine nature through creatures (Dist. 3), and knowing a nature means knowing its operation. If the Father begot by nature, they could have known the eternal generation, which was shown false.
claims: Knowing a nature entails knowing its operations.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e221.summary: Sed contra from Hilary: will gave God's substance to all creatures, but nature gave it to the Son.
claims: Hilary: creatures come from will, the Son from nature.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e227.summary: Second sed contra from Damascene: generation is a work of the divine nature.
claims: Damascene: generation is a work of the divine nature.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e233.summary: Thomas's determination. The divine essence is the principle of all divine acts, though as essence it is the principle of being rather than of operation. Since the essence includes diverse attributes, really one and conceptually distinct, an act is referred to the essence under whichever attribute the act's condition requires. Understanding is from the essence as intellect, and willed things that can be or not be are produced by it as will. Generation essentially produces the begotten in the likeness of the begetter, and the principle of such production belongs to nature, which brings forth like from like. So the Father begot the Son by nature.
claims: Acts are referred to the divine essence under the attribute their condition requires.
Generation, as production in likeness of nature, proceeds from the essence as nature.
The Father begot the Son by nature.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e236.summary: Reply to the first argument. By 'natural necessity' Hilary means something done by the power of nature contrary to the will, like hunger and thirst in us, where the will suffers a kind of violence from nature. There is no such necessity in God.
claims: Hilary's 'natural necessity' is nature acting against the will, which has no place in God.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e239.summary: Reply to the second argument. Nature and will are really the same in God but differ in concept. So the divine essence, as nature, is the principle of something of which it is not the principle as will.
claims: Nature and will in God are conceptually distinct principles.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e242.summary: Reply to the third argument. A nature can be known in two ways: by perfect comprehension, which the philosophers lacked, since that would give knowledge of all God's works; or through effects, as they did know it. Creatures do not perfectly represent the divine nature as principle of eternal and consubstantial generation, so the philosophers did not know divine generation, its operation.
claims: Knowledge of God's nature through effects does not reveal the eternal generation.

ta-l1d6q1-d1e252.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Will cannot precede wisdom' is said because wisdom is appropriated to the Son. Against the objection that the will moves the other powers and so precedes knowledge, Thomas distinguishes two acts of will. The imperfect act, desiring, precedes perfect knowledge of what is to be learned but is itself preceded by an indeterminate, universal knowledge, since what is wholly unknown is not sought. The perfect act, resting and delighting in what is had, follows perfect knowledge. (2) On whether God begot the Son willing or unwilling (volens aut nolens): these are not contradictories; 'willing' and 'not willing' are. 'Nolo' affirms an act of will directed at something's not being ('I will this not to be'), so a stone is neither willing nor unwilling. Neither is to be granted of the Father. 'Not willing' is to be granted if 'willing' means supervening or antecedent will, and 'willing he begot' if it means concomitant will.
claims: Every act of will is preceded by some knowledge; desiring precedes perfect knowledge, resting follows it.
'Volens' and 'nolens' are not contradictories; 'volens' and 'non volens' are.
The Father begot 'willing' in the sense of concomitant will.

ta-l1d6q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 6 maps Lombard's question about the principle of the Son's generation (necessity, will, or nature) and his refutation of Eunomius, and announces three articles accordingly.

ta-l1d6q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Father begot the Son by necessity. Thomas distinguishes conditional necessity, from an agent by coercion or from an end, from absolute necessity grounded in essence, which is either received from another or uncaused, as in God. Divine generation has no conditional necessity, since God is first principle and last end. It has the absolute necessity of the first cause, and Lombard's denial targets only the coercive necessity on which Eunomius's argument relied.
claims: The Son's generation is absolutely necessary, with the uncaused necessity of the first cause, but not coerced or conditioned by an end.

ta-l1d6q1-Dd1e154.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Father begot the Son by will. Thomas distinguishes will as related to its object from will as principle. The Father wills the generation as object (concomitant will), as he wills to be God. As principle, will is the formal ground of the Spirit's procession as love, and it freely produces things that can be or not be (antecedent will), which applies to creation, not to the Son, whose procession as Word corresponds to the intellect. Supervening will does not exist in God. Origen's 'offspring of will' means the Son in whom the Father's good pleasure rests.
claims: The Father begot the Son by concomitant, not antecedent, will.
Will is the principle of the Spirit's procession and of creation; intellect corresponds to the Son's generation.

ta-l1d6q1-Dd1e200.summary: Article 3 asks whether the Father begot the Son by nature. Objections cite Hilary's denial of natural necessity, the identity of will and nature, and the philosophers' knowledge of the divine nature. Thomas holds that acts are referred to the essence under the fitting attribute, and generation, as production in likeness of nature, belongs to the essence as nature: the Father begets by nature. Hilary excludes only nature acting against the will. Nature and will are conceptually distinct principles, and the philosophers knew the divine nature only through effects that do not represent it as principle of eternal generation.
claims: The Father begot the Son by nature.
Nature and will are conceptually distinct principles in God.

ta-l1d6q1-Dd1e247.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 6 explains the order of will and wisdom through imperfect desire and perfect rest of will. It analyses 'volens/nolens' as non-contradictories and concludes that the Father begot 'willing' only in the sense of concomitant will.
claims: 'Nolens' is not the contradictory of 'volens'.
The Father begot willing by concomitant will.

ta-l1d6q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 6 asks about the principle of the Son's generation. Article 1 holds that the generation is necessary with the absolute, uncaused necessity of the first cause, but not by coercion or for an end. Lombard's denial of necessity targets Eunomius's coercive sense. Article 2 holds that the Father begot the Son by will only in the sense of concomitant will, willing it as object. Will as principle grounds the Spirit's procession as love and the free production of creatures, while the Son proceeds as Word from the intellect. Article 3 holds that the Father begot by nature, since generation, as production in likeness of nature, belongs to the essence under the attribute of nature. The Expositio clarifies the order of will and knowledge and the logic of 'willing' and 'unwilling'.
claims: The Son's generation has absolute, not coercive, necessity.
The Father begot the Son by nature, and by will only concomitantly.
Creation proceeds from antecedent, free will; the Spirit proceeds as love.
